The dataset features 12 heterogeneous sensing modalities and 67.72 million synchronized frames from 41 participants performing 62 diverse activities.

author_final_remarks.value:
We sincerely thank all the reviewers for your patience and insightful feedback.  At the heart of this paper is the recognition of a significant gap: the current lack of multi-modal datasets encompassing various COTS modalities and distinct, representative human activities for real-world use. To this end, we propose OctoNet, a comprehensive benchmark featuring **12 synchronized sensing modalities** (RGB, depth, thermal, IRA, ToF, radar, etc.) from **41 participants** across **62 activities**, totaling **67.72M synchronized frames**, all **aligned to high-fidelity MoCap 3D poses**. Additionally, we integrate the pose annotations as a **shared, interpretable representation**. We believe OctoNet is not just a resource for advancing HAR and HPE, but a **critical testbed for cross-modal understanding and the development of sensing foundation models in embodied AI**. We are grateful that all the reviewers recognized these unique contributions. 

The discussion period was invaluable in improving and sharpening the paper’s contributions, focusing on two key questions: 1) how OctoNet reveals current research gaps, and 2) how it demonstrates the strength of modality fusion. For the first question, we conducted comprehensive evaluations with representative backbones, which reveal biased performance across modalities: Swin-T does not necessarily outperform CNN-based backbones despite its success in NLP and CV, highlighting significant research opportunities in designing better backbones for building foundational models across heterogeneous modalities. For the second, OctoNet enables exploration of multi-modal synergies: fusion experiments show that integrating diverse modalities yields performance gains, validating their complementarity. By including under-explored modalities like ToF/SFCW/IRA, OctoNet offers the community the most comprehensive platform for advancing multi-modal learning and cross-modal understanding.

We have provided detailed point-by-point responses to address all reviewer concerns, leading to more positive feedback and several reviewers raising their scores. All clarifications and new results will be integrated into the final manuscript, with all scripts open-sourced, the dataset fully available and usable, and ongoing maintenance ensured.

We are committed to continuously developing and maintaining OctoNet for the community. We greatly appreciate the opportunity to improve our work and sincerely hope for your support.

**[2. Clarification of SOTA Results]** We would like to clarify why, in some cases, the “SOTA” models achieve worse results than other methods in our experiments. First and foremost, as mentioned earlier, there are no exact SOTA models that have been designed or evaluated specifically for our dataset. The range of human activities and motions in OctoNet is fundamentally different from those addressed in previous tasks and datasets. As such, it is reasonable and expected that SOTA models from prior work may not consistently perform best in our benchmarking. Second, the SOTA models we benchmark against are often highly reliant on pretraining with large-scale datasets that are not directly comparable to the real-world settings presented in OctoNet. For example, Video-Swin relies on pre-training on Kinetics-400/600/SSv2 (each comprising 100K~400K videos) and HTS-AT is pre-trained on AudioSet (comprising over 2 billion frames, 4,000x larger than that in OctoNet). As observed by previous research [1, 2], Transformer excels at modeling with global self-attention, it lacks the built-in inductive biases that convolutional networks inherently possess. Transformers will show significantly superior performance only when they are pretrained on a large dataset to obtain the inductive bias [3,4]. Furthermore, the real-world complexity of our dataset presents additional challenges. OctoNet is intentionally designed to reflect daily-life scenarios: it features comprehensive camera viewpoints, highly flexible and realistic activities, and accounts for scene changes, user variability, and a wide array of ambient interferences that are characteristic of real-world applications. These aspects significantly increase the difficulty of the recognition task compared to existing datasets.

These results open up new directions for current and future research. First, OctoNet offers a rigorous benchmark for evaluating a model’s generalization and robustness in the absence of specific pre-training paradigms, as it exposes models to genuine real-world diversity and challenging conditions. Second, as we emphasize in our paper, OctoNet's high-fidelity 3D pose labels provide a unified and interpretable "universal language" for all 12 modalities. This allows researchers to explore advanced topics such as cross-modal supervision and novel multi-modal fusion strategies. Third, these unique advantages, combined with its unprecedented modal breadth and data scale, pave the way for developing and evaluating the next generation of Sensing Foundation Models. We believe this will help shift the community’s focus from optimizing for narrow, task-specific benchmarks toward building truly general-purpose and robust perceptual intelligence.

Thank you again for your detailed review and critical feedback on our work. This feedback has been invaluable for improving the quality of our paper. We must apologize for the delay in our response. Upon receiving your comments, our team was genuinely surprised by the inconsistencies and took your feedback very seriously. Given the complexity of our experiments and the breadth of the modalities involved, we felt it was essential to conduct a thorough, careful and responsible investigation before this response. We want to ensure that every aspect has been rigorously checked, so we could provide you with an accurate and comprehensive explanation.

Over the past two days, our team initiated a systematic internal review. This process involved:

- Re-examining all implementations and experiment code, including any recent modifications made for the addition of new SOTA baselines.
- Carefully reviewing experiment logs and result records to search for any anomalies or signs of misconfiguration.
- Comparing outputs across different runs and cross-referencing them with the results reported in both the main paper and supplementary materials.
- Evaluating data processing pipelines, random seed settings, and model checkpoints to identify potential sources of inconsistency.
- Discussing findings within the team and retracing each step for any overlooked details or human errors.

Throughout this process, we systematically ruled out various potential causes of the issues. After thorough analysis and discussion, we finally **pinpoint the root causes** of the discrepancies you identified. **Importantly, the results in the main submission are accurate and were not affected.** We have documented these findings in detail and will address each issue specifically in the following sections.

**[1. Implementation of SOTA Models]** We would like to clarify several important details regarding our experimental setup for the SOTA methods, which may have led to some confusing results. First, it is important to note that OctoNet is the first large-scale multi-modal dataset covering 62 distinct human activities, and its downstream tasks differ significantly from those addressed in existing works. We appreciate the suggestion to benchmark against SOTA models, and for the purpose of this study, we **define a SOTA model as the best-performing model utilizing a particular modality**, even if the downstream task diverges from our own.  After thorough and detailed surveys of the related work, we identify the SOTA work for the following modality: SCL-SwinT (UWB), FOCAL (IMU), HTS-AT (Audio) and Video-Swin (Video). Among these, both SCL-SwinT and FOCAL adopt a contrastive learning framework for training. FOCAL introduces a multi-modal architecture for time-series data, while SCL-SwinT further incorporates similarity embeddings to enable supervised contrastive learning. For HTS-AT (Audio), their token-semantic CNN is specifically tailored for other downstream tasks, i.e. event detection, which is different from our HAR task. These frameworks often require specific loss functions, complex positive/negative pair sampling strategies, and multi-stage training pipelines. It was thus not feasible to fully reproduce these SOTA frameworks on our dataset within the limited time and computational resources available, particularly as we prioritized multimodal fusion experiments to highlight the complementary nature of our dataset’s modalities. Consequently, we did not fully reproduce all SOTA methods for those that rely on complex self-supervised or contrastive learning frameworks. Conversely, we **take a pragmatic strategy** to evaluate the SOTA model. Specifically, for SCL-SwinT (UWB), FOCAL (IMU) and HTS-AT (Audio), we used their encoders as feature extractors, converting our data to the appropriate input format as described in the original papers. We then appended a unified fully-connected output layer and trained the entire model from scratch for our specific supervised learning task. For RGB, since Video-Swin takes video as the input, we faithfully reimplemented this framework and train it thoroughly for both 10 and 62 classes.

During implementation, we find FOCAL and HTS-AT have open-sourced their code, while SCL-SwinT has not. We carefully investigate the code for FOCAL and HTS-AT, and observe the encoders share the Swin-T architecture. The SCL-SwinT also clearly claims that they directly adopt the Swin-T for encoding. Therefore, the SOTA model results you observed for these three modalities are equivalent to the results on their **core Swin-T backbone.**  We apologize for not explaining this point clearly in our previous communication and for any misunderstanding this caused.

Thank you for the reply.

The provided experiments with SOTA methods bring additional questions and concerns.

$\textbf{[Results with SOTA]}$

Why do the SOTA methods significantly underperform very simple baselines (ResNet, DenseNet, etc.)?

When comparing the provided result of ID (10/62-classes) with Table 3 in the paper, the SOTA methods show significant performance drops in almost all cases.

- RGB (10 classes): DenseNet (94.3%) vs. Video Swin (93.4%)

- IMU (10 classes): ResNet (98.4%) vs. DenseNet (98.4%) vs. FOCAL (95.3%)

- IMU (62 classes): ResNet (96.6%) vs. FOCAL (89.6%)

- UWB (62 classes): ResNet (95.0%) vs. SCL-SwinT (90.5%)

- Audio (10 classes): DenseNet (60.0%) vs. HTS-AT (36.6%)

- Audio  (10 classes): DenseNet (54.9%) vs. HTS-AT (32.1%)

This performance drop can also be observed in CU and CS, as shown in the newly provided results and Table 1 in the supplementary PDF.

Why do the SOTA methods fail on the proposed OctoNet dataset? This question could also be related to my initial comment: "An important question that remains unaddressed is: Are there limitations or blind spots in current SOTA models that OctoNet helps reveal?".


$\textbf{[Clarification of Some Strange Results with SOAT]}$

**[SOTA Baselines and Multimodal Tasks]** Thank you for raising this important point. We fully agree that extending the experimental scope to include stronger baselines and diverse learning tasks is critical to demonstrate the full utility of OctoNet.

To that end, we incorporate SOTA baselines for well-studied modalities in human activity recognition (HAR), as summarized below:

| MODALITIES | SOTA Model | ID (10/62-classes) | CU (10/62-classes) | CS (10/62-classes) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RGB | Video Swin [1] | 93.4±2.3  / 91.8±1.0 | 27.5±3.1 / 5.0±0.6 | 11.6±2.7 / 2.0±0.4 |
| IMU | FOCAL [2] | 95.3±1.9 / 89.6±1.1 | 76.3±2.9 / 37.2±1.3 | 60.4±4.2 / 27.7±1.5 |
| UWB | SCL-SwinT [3] | 99.2±0.8 / 90.5±1.0 | 16.3±2.6 / 2.5±0.4  | 15.9±3.0 / 1.3±0.4 |
| Audio | HTS-AT [4]  | 36.6±4.4 / 32.1±1.7 | 25.4±3.1 / 8.1±0.8 | 13.5±2.8 / 2.0±0.5 |

These results reflect strong baseline performance across modalities, particularly for in-domain inference. However, we also observe significant performance drops under cross-user and cross-scene settings, even with SOTA models. This reveals a persistent generalization gap, highlighting an unresolved challenge in current HAR methods. OctoNet provides a platform to investigate this issue further and encourages the development of more robust models for real-world deployment.

To explore OctoNet’s multi-modal potential, we performed preliminary fusion experiments on the 10-class subset with complementary modalities:

| Fused Modality | Model | In-Domain | Cross-User | Cross-Scene |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RGB, FMCW, Acoustic | DenseNet | 99.2 | 66.5 | 39.8 |
| Depth, ToF, UWB, WiFi | ResNet | 99.2 | 46.9 | 29.0 |
| Thermal, IRA, IMU | ResNet | 99.9 | 75.2 | 52.7 |

We use pretrained unimodal encoders and concatenate their feature maps, which are then passed to a fully connected layer for classification. These fusion setups demonstrate substantial gains over unimodal models, particularly for complex activities or scenarios with missing/incomplete data. For example:

- Thermal + IRA help disambiguate fine-grained activities (e.g., drawing a zigzag vs. drawing a circle), where IMU alone captures similar motion magnitudes but not the spatial or heat-distribution patterns.
- Radar-based modalities (UWB, FMCW) complement vision in low-light or occluded conditions.
- Audio, while weak alone, boosts robustness when fused with visual and motion-based signals.

These results emphasize the complementarity among modalities across spatial, temporal, and spectral dimensions, validating OctoNet’s capacity to support advanced fusion research, such as attention-based fusion, modality dropout, or cross-modal alignment.

In addition to HAR and pose estimation, OctoNet is well-positioned to support a range of emerging tasks, such as:

- Domain adaptation and generalization across subjects and environments
- Cross-modal retrieval and representation learning
- Foundation model pretraining for physical world understanding

The dataset’s scale, diversity, and fine-grained alignment across 12 modalities create an ideal testbed for studying these challenges systematically.

**[Activity Distribution Statistics]** Thank you for pointing this out. OctoNet includes 62 diverse activity classes, and we have carefully ensured a balanced class distribution across the dataset. Specifically, the proportion of each class ranges from 1.45% to 1.62%, with an average close to 1.61% (i.e., 1/62). This balance is achieved by having all 41 participants perform every activity multiple times under a standardized collection protocol, ensuring uniform coverage across subjects and classes.

We will make this distribution explicitly clear in the revised manuscript and refer to the detailed breakdown provided in the "Metadata of OctoNet Dataset" section of our GitHub repository, where per-class instance counts are documented. This balanced design supports fair and unbiased training for supervised learning tasks and provides a reliable basis for benchmarking generalization performance across modalities and conditions.

**[Origin of the Name “OctoNet”]** We’re glad you asked! The name “OctoNet” is inspired by both technical and cultural aspects:

1. Technically, the dataset initially included 8 core sensing modalities, connected by a common 3D pose representation via motion capture. This architecture reminded us of an octopus, with sensory “arms” reaching into different domains (visual, acoustic, RF, inertial, etc.), all linked to a shared body of pose data.
2. Culturally, our team is based in Hong Kong, where the Octopus Card is widely used as a connector for transportation, commerce, and services. Similarly, OctoNet connects diverse sensing channels to form a unified network for understanding human activity.

**[Code Accessibility]** We understand your concern regarding the baseline code availability. As per NeurIPS Author Response guidelines, we are currently not permitted to modify our public repositories during the review process. However, we have already released:

- The full dataset and modality loaders
- Visualization tools
- Metadata

Upon paper acceptance, we commit to releasing complete configuration files and training scripts for all baselines, enabling full reproducibility and extension by the research community.

[1]. Liu, Ze, et al. "Video swin transformer." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition*. 2022.

[2]. Liu, Shengzhong, et al. "Focal: Contrastive learning for multimodal time-series sensing signals in factorized orthogonal latent space." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 36 (2023): 47309-47338.

[3]. Li, Xiaoxiong, et al. "Advancing IR-UWB radar human activity recognition with swin transformers and supervised contrastive learning." *IEEE Internet of Things Journal* 11.7 (2023): 11750-11766.

[4]. Chen, Ke, et al. "Hts-at: A hierarchical token-semantic audio transformer for sound classification and detection." *ICASSP 2022-2022 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)*. IEEE, 2022.

Thank you very much for your detailed and thoughtful feedback. We address your concerns in turn below:

**[Mocap Suits and Indoor Environment Limitations]** We acknowledge the limitations introduced by the use of standardized mocap suits and the constraint of indoor studio settings. Our primary goal with OctoNet is to enable multi-modal fusion and alignment research at scale. A key novelty of the dataset is the inclusion of high-fidelity 3D MoCap pose annotations, which serve not only as a supervisory signal for pose estimation tasks but also as a common intermediate representation to facilitate cross-modal learning. As you noted, obtaining synchronized data from such a wide range of modalities is highly impractical in unconstrained environments. Recent multi-modal datasets such as mRI [1] and MM-Fi [2] also rely on indoor settings for similar reasons. We appreciate your understanding in this regard. Nonetheless, we agree that combining our dataset with in-the-wild, single-modality datasets (e.g., RGB or IMU-based) represents an important research direction for improving generalization. Our dataset provides a controlled, richly annotated foundation that can complement these more varied sources.

**[Baseline Experiment Details]** We confirm that our activity recognition experiments are **not performed on a per-frame basis**. Instead, we use **sequences of consecutive frames** as model inputs. Each modality provides time-aligned data, which we group into temporal windows during training and evaluation. This structure allows the models to learn both **spatial and temporal features**. Additional implementation details, including the temporal input structure, are reflected in our open-source codebase (e.g., shape_converter.py), and we will release full configuration files for all baseline models after the review period.

**[Pose Estimation – MPJPE Clarification]** Thank you for your insightful question regarding the pose estimation results in Table 4. We clarify that the reported **MPJPE values are computed in the global coordinate system and are not root-relative**. This setup reflects absolute 3D joint error from the MoCap ground truth rather than relative joint positions centered at the root (e.g., pelvis). As a result, the reported errors are naturally higher than typical root-relative benchmarks.

Several factors contribute to these elevated MPJPE values:

- **Global Pose Annotations**: Since the 3D pose labels are provided in a global scene-aligned coordinate frame (captured via OptiTrack), the model must infer not only joint configurations but also global body translation. This is especially challenging for modalities with limited spatial resolution or field-of-view (e.g., IR Array, ToF), which exacerbates localization errors.
- **Viewpoint and Scene Complexity**: Unlike datasets with fixed front-facing camera views, OctoNet includes data from multiple sensor viewpoints around the subject. This increases variability in appearance and background context, making spatial generalization more difficult.
- **Model Initialization**: For RGB-based pose estimation, we trained ResNet-style backbones from scratch. As the reviewer suggests, using **ImageNet-pretrained models** could offer better generalization and alleviate background overfitting issues mentioned in L251. We agree with this suggestion and will include such results in the revised version.

For more niche modalities (e.g., radar, thermal, WiFi), pretrained models are generally unavailable. However, this highlights an important motivation behind OctoNet: enabling the development and benchmarking of robust pose estimation techniques for underexplored sensing modalities and scenarios where pretraining is not yet feasible.

We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point and will make the MPJPE definition and experimental setup more explicit in the final manuscript.

**[Clarification of Frame Counts in Table 1]** We appreciate you flagging the ambiguity in Table 1. The current “#Frames” column aggregates frame counts across all modalities and might indeed be misinterpreted as each modality containing 67 million frames. We will **revise the caption** to explicitly state that the total reflects the **cumulative count across all modalities**, not per modality.

**[Placement of Sound Modality in Fig. 1]** Thank you for pointing this out. While our intention was to illustrate all modalities along a common “signal spectrum,” we agree that placing

**sound** on the electromagnetic spectrum is misleading. In the revision, we will **disconnect the sound modality** (as we already do for heart rate) to avoid confusion.

**[Terminology: Cross-User vs. Cross-Subject]** Thank you for this suggestion. We agree that **“Cross-Subject”** is more appropriate, especially when the participants are not direct users of any system. We will update the terminology accordingly throughout the paper.

**[Code Accessibility]** As mentioned in the manuscript and above, the **data loading and visualization code is already available**. Due to the NeurIPS author response policy, we are currently unable to modify the repository during the review period. However, we commit to releasing **all baseline training scripts and configuration files** immediately upon acceptance to support full reproducibility.

We really appreciate the insightful feedback. We will clarify them as follows: 

**[Alignment and Generalization]** Our initial focus on temporal alignment stems from the fact that all modalities in our setup, such as RGB-D, RF, IMU, and audio, are inherently time-synchronized with respect to human activities. Synchronizing these signals temporally is essential to ensure consistent and meaningful cross-modal correspondence within the dataset. We fully acknowledge, however, the significance of spatial alignment given that sensors may observe actions from different viewpoints or positions, which can result in heterogeneous outputs. To address this, we specifically incorporate human pose as an intermediate representation for activity recognition. Human pose provides a unified and physically grounded description of the activity, effectively bridging spatial discrepancies across modalities. In this context, we utilize OptiTrack to obtain precise 3D pose annotations as additional labels, ensuring that downstream models can anchor their spatial understanding of activities, irrespective of sensor layout.

On the other hand, Utilizing pose as an intermediate representation can mitigate issues arising from changes in sensor layout, as pose estimation serves as a spatially consistent anchor. However, we acknowledge that fully robust cross-layout generalization remains a challenging open problem; our dataset provides the foundation for exploring these questions, and we hope to spur further research on spatial calibration and sensor invariance in multimodal HAR and HPE. 

**[Modality Fusion]** Additionally, as for the fusion of those modalities, we provide a preliminary study on the 10-class subset by fusing the complementary modalities as follows:

| Fused Modality | Model | In-Domain | Cross-User | Cross-Scene |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RGB, FMCW, Acoustic | DenseNet | 99.2 | 66.5 | 39.8 |
| Depth, ToF, UWB, WiFi | ResNet | 99.2 | 46.9 | 29.0 |
| Thermal, IRA, IMU | ResNet | 99.9 | 75.2 | 52.7 |

Specifically, we use the trained single modality model as the encoder and concat the feature maps and pass to the FC layer. From the above, we can tell, the inclusion of thermal and IRA  is helpful for IMU to distinguish between activities such as drawing a zigzag and drawing a circle. While IMU data may only capture similar wrist or arm movement magnitudes for both actions, the thermal or IRA modality provides distinctive patterns of heat distribution and contact dynamics associated with each gesture. For example, the intermittent stops and sharp turns when drawing a zigzag result in different thermal signatures compared to the smoother, continuous motion of drawing a circle.  Similarly, when distinguishing between drawing a circle and kicking, the depth modality alone may be insufficient; however, other modalities such as UWB, ToF, and Wi-Fi offer additional, highly informative cues. These complementary signals enable the fusion model to successfully disambiguate activities that are ambiguous to individual modalities. 

These results underscore that different modalities convey complementary information, e.g. spatial, temporal, frequency. When effectively fused, these features can produce stronger results than single-modality approaches alone. This, in turn, raises important research opportunities: for example, how to optimally combine multiple modalities for robust activity recognition. We believe OctoNet provides an unprecedented resource for the community to explore and address these critical questions. 

Regarding the observation that ResNet outperforms RFNet on IMU signals, we believe this is mainly because IMU-based activity recognition relies heavily on capturing local temporal fluctuations, such as rapid changes in acceleration and angular velocity. ResNet excels at extracting these localized temporal features and short-term dependencies, making it particularly well-suited for this type of data.

In contrast, RFNet is specifically designed for data with complex spatial structures, such as RF images or heatmaps, and is less optimized for the more regular, sequential signal patterns found in IMU data. Therefore, for IMU-based tasks, the ability to capture fine-grained, local temporal variations is crucial.

**[Motivation]** While most of the current research in embodied AI centers on video, audio and IMU, we envision that the inclusion of numerous RF sensors will significantly enlarge the boundaries of perceptions. That is why we make this dataset available. As shown in Tab.1, no existing resource simultaneously offers diverse spectrum of electromagnetic and non-electormagnetic signals and full‑body 3D Pose ground truth. Each modality offers unique properties: for instance, cameras provide rich visual context but struggle with occlusion or low-light conditions, while RF-based modalities such as WiFi and UWB are robust to these challenges and offer enhanced privacy, since they do not capture visual imagery. The incorporation of these many common off-the-shelf at home would be a great opportunity to explore the integration between these modalities, especially when integrated communication and sensing (ISAC) will be the standard for the next-generation wireless network. On the other hand, these RF modalities have already been shown achieve strong, privacy‑friendly HAR. Concretely, the inclusion of WiFi and UWB is well-justified by a growing body of literature. For example, WiFi-based HAR has been shown to achieve competitive or even superior performance to traditional approaches under challenging scenarios, with works like Person-in-WiFi 3D [1], RF-Pose [2], Widar 3.0 [3], WiPose [4], GoPose [5], OPERAnet [6], MM‑Fi [7] and XRF55 [8] demonstrating accurate device-free HAR and even precise 3D pose estimation using only commodity routers. Similarly, the unique characteristics of UWB, such as centimeter-level ranging accuracy and large coverage, have made it a focus in recent HAR research and public datasets, as seen in Bocus UWB [9], Opportunity++ [10], and OPERAnet [6].  By aligning a diverse range of signals, OctoNet supports a wide spectrum of research tasks, including human activity recognition, 3D pose estimation, multi-modal fusion, cross-modal alignment, and the development of foundation models for physical sensing.

We hope these justifications will address your concerns.

Thanks for your valuable and insightful comments. We will address your concerns as follows:

**[Benchmark]** As stated in our paper, the reason we choose to leverage those backbone is two folds. First, many of these modalities have not established a recognized SOTA backbone in the human activity recognition and human pose estimation, and none of them has included such a comprehensive set of human activities in their training. A key contribution of our work is the first-time alignment and benchmarking of these diverse modalities and activities with synchronized ground truth, thus establishing a fair and unified platform for cross-modality and cross-activity comparison. Moreover, these baselines appear as the fundamental backbones in the AI era. In other words, the current SOTA model rely on the ResNet-like [1][2][3], Transformer-like [4][5] structures.  While well-established SOTA models do exist for specific modalities (such as video, audio, IMU, and UWB), we adopt them to provide a representative and competitive benchmark. Our results are summarized below:

| MODALITIES | SOTA Model | ID (10/62-classes) | CU (10/62-classes) | CS (10/62-classes) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RGB | Video Swin [6] | 93.4±2.3  / 91.8±1.0 | 27.5±3.1 / 5.0±0.6 | 11.6±2.7 / 2.0±0.4 |
| IMU | FOCAL [7] | 95.3±1.9 / 89.6±1.1 | 76.3±2.9 / 37.2±1.3 | 60.4±4.2 / 27.7±1.5 |
| UWB | SCL-SwinT [8] | 99.2±0.8 / 90.5±1.0 | 16.3±2.6 / 2.5±0.4  | 15.9±3.0 / 1.3±0.4 |
| Audio | HTS-AT [9]  | 36.6±4.4 / 32.1±1.7 | 25.4±3.1 / 8.1±0.8 | 13.5±2.8 / 2.0±0.5 |

As seen from above, we leverage the Video Swin [6] as the SOTA model for RGB-based human activity recognition. We train the model from scratch. The RGB data achieves the in-domain accuracy of 93.4%. This demonstrates the quality of our models that can easily evaluate the single-modality performances. Similarly, we leverage FOCAL [7] as the SOTA model for IMU and it achieves the accuracy of 95.3 for 10-class in-domain inference. For UWB, we employ SCL-SwinT [8], which derives from Swin-T, as the SOTA and it reaches accuracy of 99.2%. As for the audio, we pick the recent SOTA work on audio event classification HTS-AT [9] as the SOTA model. It is worse than the other three modalities because many of the activities included are not distinguishable solely by sound, which should be addressed by incorporating other modalities. 

We also observe notable modality-specific strengths. For instance, IMU excels at distinguishing activities with prominent temporal patterns, such as walking, bowing, and dancing, while thermal sensors are particularly effective for activities like drawing, which rely more on spatial features. These results underscore the importance of leveraging complementary modality characteristics for enhanced recognition.

More importantly, our dataset enables the identification of several promising future research directions. For example, all modalities exhibit a marked drop in performance for cross-user and cross-scene generalization, even with SOTA backbones, indicating that current SOTA models still struggle to address real-world variability. This opens up important avenues for developing new models and strategies to improve generalization across users and environments.

**[Modality Fusion]** To further validate the performance of cross-modality fusion, we conduct a preliminary experiment on the 10-class subset to showcase the fusion. 

| Fused Modality | Model | In-Domain | Cross-User | Cross-Scene |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RGB, FMCW, Acoustic | DenseNet | 99.2 | 66.5 | 39.8 |
| Depth, ToF, UWB, WiFi  | ResNet | 99.2 | 46.9  | 29.0 |
| Thermal, IRA, IMU | ResNet | 99.9 | 75.2 | 52.7 |

As shown above, the fusion can significantly boost the in-domain accuracy. For example, audio by itself has difficulty distinguishing activities such as dancing, as these activities do not have distinctive acoustic features. However, when audio is combined with FMCW radar and RGB input, the fused model benefits from additional spatial and movement-based cues, including information about color, range, velocity, and body displacement.  

Notably, these results help uncover the gaps of the current research. Visual-based recognition can be strengthened by integrating radar signals that remain reliable even when the scene contains occlusions. On the other hand, sensors that capture movement dynamics, such as IMU, work particularly well when used together with thermal or infrared sensing, as these modalities offer unique spatial information that is hard to obtain otherwise. While our preliminary fusion approach delivers notable improvements, it is likely that more sophisticated fusion strategies can further enhance performance. Future research could examine methods such as attention mechanisms or context-driven feature weighting to fully capitalize on the rich set of complementary information available from these multiple sensing modalities.

**[Significance of OctoNet]** To the best of our knowledge, OctoNet is the first dataset that covers these comprehensive perception modalities with large scale, diverse coverage of subjects, activities, sensing conditions and modalities. This enables research of cross-modality that are not feasible with any existing dataset. Our baseline experiments highlight two key findings: (1) State-of-the-art backbone models achieve strong results across individual modalities, demonstrating the dataset’s quality and making it a valuable resource for benchmarking single-modal as well as cross-modal methods; (2) There is significant performance drop when applying in cross-user and cross-scene conditions, suggesting that domain shift remains a significant challenge even for leading models. 

Crucially, OctoNet provides high-fidelity, motion-capture-based 3D pose annotations for all cases, which can act as a universal and interpretable common ground across modalities, facilitating not only 3D pose estimation, but also deeper investigation into shared representations and multi-modal perception. Rather than competing solely as a benchmark for HAR or HPE, OctoNet is designed to advance research into how diverse sensing modalities can be fused and leveraged in unison for robust activity recognition and beyond. This multi-modal context, alignment, and explicit bridging via human pose are features that, to our knowledge, are unmatched in current datasets.

**[Code Accessibility]** All the data and the corresponding data loaders are available in the repo. We will open-source all the detailed configuration files and all necessary resources to ensure full reproducibility of our baseline experiments.

**References:**

summary.value:
The paper presents OctoNet, a large-scale, multi-modal, multi-view dataset for human activity understanding and multi-modal learning. OctoNet supports a wide range of tasks such as activity recognition, 3D pose estimation, multi-modal fusion, and cross-modal learning, and serves as a comprehensive benchmark for building generalizable and robust human-centric AI models. 

The dataset includes synchronized data from 12 diverse sensor modalities (e.g., RGB, depth, thermal, radar, Wi-Fi, IMU, audio) captured across 41 participants performing 62 varied activities, resulting in over 67.72 million frames. In particular, the ground truths of these data modalities come from high-precision 3D pose annotations using a mocap system.

The paper shows extensive baseline experiments with common architectures (ResNet, DenseNet, and RFNet) to demonstrate the dataset's utility.

strengths_contributions.value:
As shown in Table 1, the proposed dataset is large with a wide variety of sensing modalities. This can be helpful for multi-modal learning and building a foundational model for understanding human activities.

The subjects are quite diverse in terms of age, height, weight, gender, and nationality.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
I'm not fully convinced by the main reasons for not using SOTA methods in the experimental evaluations:

- L220: several modalities, especially IRAs and ToF sensors, are relatively underexplored, with no well-established models available.
- L221-223: we aim to ensure a consistent and fair comparison across modalities by using architectures with flexible input handling and minimal modality-specific engineering. 

A comparison across modalities can be valuable, particularly for highlighting the strengths and limitations of different sensor types. However, they do not justify "not benchmarking against SOTA methods", especially where such methods exist and are widely used (e.g., well-studied modalities like RGB, depth, and IMU, where strong baselines already exist). Why do we specifically prefer a comparison across different modalities with very simple models to a comparison with SOTA methods? Comparing across modalities might help answer which sensors are more informative or robust, but benchmarking against SOTA models is essential to answer how well this dataset supports progress on established tasks. These two types of comparisons are complementary, not mutually exclusive. Including the comparison with SOTA methods would strengthen the experimental rigor and position OctoNet more clearly within the broader landscape of human activity datasets.

An important question that remains unaddressed is: Are there limitations or blind spots in current SOTA models that OctoNet helps reveal? For example, does the dataset expose modality-specific challenges or generalization gaps that prior datasets could not capture? Addressing this would not only justify the data compositions but also better articulate the unique contributions and value of OctoNet.

Additionally, a central strength of the OctoNet dataset lies in its diverse set of sensor modalities, which offers a rare opportunity to explore multi-modal learning at scale. However, the paper does not include any baseline models that explicitly leverage the full set (or at least some sets) of multi-modal inputs. Including even a simple model that fuses multiple modalities would have helped validate the dataset’s utility and provided a stronger foundation for future work.

Furthermore, while OctoNet is comprehensive in its modality coverage, individual aspects of the dataset are less competitive with existing benchmarks for certain tasks. For example, in 3D human pose estimation, the data lack in-the-wild collection conditions and show limited variation in clothing and scene diversity. As a result, OctoNet is unlikely to serve as a primary benchmark for pose estimation, where realism and generalization to unconstrained environments are critical. In this context, demonstrating the value of OctoNet through multi-modal baseline experiments (mentioned above) becomes even more critical to underscore what this dataset offers that others do not.

final_justification.value:
First of all, I can see the value of the multi-modal baseline experiments (as I suggested in the initial review to highlight the value of the dataset in the absence of SOTA experiments), which were delivered by the authors in their rebuttal. Also, the rebuttal is satisfactory to resolve my concerns. Therefore, I’m willing to raise my score.

However, as the authors mentioned in the reply, there were a significant number of mistakes in the paper and explanations. Thus, I would like to leave some comments regarding these issues.

$\textbf{[Results with SOTA]}$

The authors mentioned the following in the rebuttal.

- We leverage the Video Swin [6] as the SOTA model
- We leverage FOCAL [7] as the SOTA model for IMU
- For UWB, we employ SCL-SwinT [8], which derives from Swin-T, as the SOTA
- As for the audio, we pick the recent SOTA work on audio event classification HTS-AT [9] as the SOTA model

Based on these statements and the provided table with the column of “SOTA model”, most readers/reviewers would simply believe that the authors DID use the SOTA models for their experiments, not the backbone encoder (i.e., Swin-T).

I strongly suggest that the authors should definitely work on the wording of the explanation, not only for this review but also for future submissions, as I believe this could significantly deceive the reviewer’s perspective.

$\textbf{[Discrepancies of Reported Results]}$

I agree with the authors that the openness about these issues is essential for verifiable science, and I’m glad that the authors carefully checked the implementation and the logging process to correct the mistakes in the rebuttal phase, with the promise of preparing a complete codebase.

summary.value: This paper presents OctoNet, a large-scale, richly annotated multi-modal dataset designed to advance human activity understanding and multi-sensor learning. The dataset features 12 heterogeneous sensing modalities—including RGB-D, thermal, ToF, radar, Wi-Fi, IMU, and more—captured across 67.72 million synchronized frames from 41 participants performing 62 diverse activities. Importantly, all modalities are aligned with high-fidelity 3D human poses obtained from a motion-capture system, serving as both supervision signals and a common representation for cross-modal learning. The dataset is publicly available via HuggingFace, accompanied by a user-friendly website and toolbox, making it a valuable resource for benchmarking a wide range of tasks such as human activity recognition, 3D pose estimation, modality fusion, and cross-modal generalization.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.	The dataset covers more than ten sensing modalities, and all streams are temporally aligned, which will greatly benefit future multimodal research.
2.	The data portal is well designed; the full dataset is open-sourced on HuggingFace and easy to download.
3.	The overall workload is substantial; collecting and aligning such rich multimodal data is inherently difficult.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.	The paper seems to report only temporal alignment. Because some sensors observe the same action from different directions or positions, their outputs can differ. Were sensor poses also spatially calibrated? If not, how should the modalities be fused, and will models trained on the current data fail when sensor layouts change? Please clarify the generalisation ability of un-calibrated data.
2.	In the experiments each modality is first rendered as a 2-D “graph” and then trained individually with common backbones such as ResNet and DenseNet. This confirms that every modality is useful, but offers limited insight into multimodal fusion. The paper also lacks analysis of phenomena such as ResNet outperforming RFNet on IMU signals—whether due to architecture or data distribution. The experimental analysis only provides a textual description of the performance of different modalities shown in the tables, lacking in-depth analysis of certain phenomena and fails to offer insightful guidance or interpretations based on the experimental results.
3.	The inclusion of 12 different modalities may be overly redundant. It is necessary to analyze whether each of these modalities is appropriate and effective for the HAR (Human Activity Recognition) task. For example, the necessity of using data such as WiFi and UWB for human activity understanding should be discussed. Citing relevant prior works could help justify your inclusion. At present, the paper does not clearly convey the importance of certain modalities—such as WiFi—in the context of HAR.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: No. There are no significant ethical concerns identified in this work. The data collection process appears to follow standard protocols, and no sensitive or personally identifiable information is involved. The research focuses on technical advancements without introducing potential risks to individuals or society.

dataset_code_comments.value: Their dataset website is well-designed, and the dataset has been uploaded to HuggingFace, allowing for direct download.

additional_feedback.value: I believe collecting such a dataset must have required significant effort. However, having so many modalities may give the impression of redundancy. It would be helpful if the authors could explain the importance of each modality to clarify their individual contributions.

final_justification.value:
The authors address my main concern about generalization under layout shifts.
The added investigations and clearer discussion of multimodal fusion provide more substantive insights.
The authors show that each modality contributes a distinct benefit and substantiate these roles with relevant literature, including for WiFi/UWB.
Overall, these additions substantially resolve my earlier doubts. I will raise my rating.

summary.value:
This paper presents a new dataset, OctoNet, for multimodal 3D human pose estimation and activity classification. The main distinguishing feature of this dataset over previous works is the use of 12 sensor modalities, while typical datasets include between 1 and 3. This includes WiFi, thermal, infrared and acoustics and more. The dataset is captured in 3 rooms, with 41 subjects, includes 62 activities and a total of 7.8 million RGB frames.
The authors define evaluation splits and protocols for pose estimation and activity classification, and evaluate several baselines using these protocols.

strengths_contributions.value:
This dataset contains the most simultaneously recorded modalities for human pose and activity recognition to date. This allows detailed analysis of multimodal techniques, modality translation, privileged learning etc., making it useful for many potential future research projects.

The number of subjects (41) appears sufficient for useful experiments, and the demographic breakdown shows diversity regarding age, gender, height, weight and ethnicity. There are multiple scenes (3), and many different activity classes (21).

The authors define useful evaluation protocols and splits to analyze cross-scene and cross-subject generalization.

The paper is well-structured and the tables provide all essential information on what data is provided. The paper is also well written in general.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
As mentioned at L277, all subjects wear standardized mocap suits in the recording. This is a considerable limitation that limits possible conclusions regarding real-world generalization. As further acknowledged by the authors, the data is also all from indoor studios, which is another limitation. However, I do understand that obtaining so many modalities would be highly impractical in the wild.

The baseline experiments are not described in enough detail. Is activity recognition done on a per-frame basis? If yes, why? The models are not fully described either.

Regarding the pose experiments, it is unclear if MPJPE root-relative. If yes, the error numbers presented in Table 4 appear unusually high (all above 130 mm and often several hundred). What could be the reason for this? L251 mentions possible overfitting to the background. It might be useful to try pretrained RGB networks as well (e.g. ImageNet-pretrained ResNet). I understand that no such pretrained networks may exist for more niche modalities, but it would be good to understand the reason for the quite high errors.

In Tab. 1, the #Frame for this dataset seems a bit misleading to me, since it sums up across all the different modalities. One can easily misunderstand it as the dataset providing all modalities for 67M frames each. This should be more clear in the caption.

To Fig. 1: Since sound is not an electromagnetic wave, it makes no sense to place it on that spectrum. It can be left unconnected, like heart rate is already.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Code is available for downloading, loading and visualizing the data. However, the code for the reproducing the baseline experiments is not provided.

additional_feedback.value:
L201: instead of Cross-User, I find the term "Cross-Subject" more appropriate, since the subject is not always a "user".


On balance, I tend towards recommending acceptance because the large number of modalities provides something unique for the community. At the same time, I see it close to the borderline, due to the limitations caused by the mocap suit and the relatively small number of scenes and the overfitting observed in the experiments, indicating perhaps that the amount and variability of the data is too little for training-from-scratch experiments.

final_justification.value: The rebuttal clarified that the MPJPE is in absolute terms, not root-relative, hence the numbers are more in line with expectations. Overall, the 12 synchronized modalities within one dataset offer a unique novelty for cross-modal/multi-modal research, and hence I would recommend acceptance, even if the provided baselines aren't at SOTA levels.

summary.value: This paper introduces a large-scale, multi-modal, and multi-view human activity dataset (OctoNet). Data are collected from 41 participants under multi-view sensor setups with various sensor modalities, containing the data of diverse daily activities with 3D pose labels. This dataset can be utilized for various tasks, e.g., activity recognition, 3D pose estimation, and multi-modal fusion.

strengths_contributions.value:
This is a comprehensive dataset that holds great value for the study of human activities and multi-modality.

1.	The dataset has a wide coverage in many aspects. The activity classes are not restricted to common daily activities under strict protocols, covering freestyle actions that are important for the generalization in real-world tasks. The sensor modalities are comprehensive. The participants show balanced gender and wide ranges of age, height, and weight, offering diversity in the study of personal activity patterns.

2.	The additional annotations of 3D poses are useful for real-world applications, which could help the deeper understanding of human activities.

3.	The dataset is evaluated on many commonly adopted models, where high accuracy shows the quality of the collected data in representing human activities.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.	Although the current evaluation is sufficient for human activity recognition and pose estimation, more state-of-the-art baselines and more diverse tasks like domain adaptation, and multi-modal methods could be included to evaluate the collected data. These could show whether the dataset poses unresolved challenges for future studies in various applications. 

2.	More statistics should be provided on the dataset, e.g., the portion of different activity classes (to show whether the data are class-balanced).

3.	Out of curiosity, why call it "OctoNet"?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The codes of the implemented baselines seem to be unavailable.

final_justification.value: My concerns are addressed by the rebuttal of the authors. The dataset is well-balanced and well-evaluated, given the additional statistics and added baselines. I keep my original positive evaluation of the submission as the final rating.

title.value: OctoNet: A Large-Scale Multi-Modal Dataset for Human Activity Understanding Grounded in Motion-Captured 3D Pose Labels

TLDR.value: A multimodal human activity and pose dataset for diversify sensing including acoustic, RF-based, vision-based, inertial, and physiological modalities

abstract.value: We introduce OctoNet, a large-scale, multi-modal, multi-view human activity dataset designed to advance human activity understanding and multi-modal learning. OctoNet comprises 12 heterogeneous modalities (including RGB, depth, thermal cameras, infrared arrays, audio, millimeter-wave radar, Wi-Fi, IMU, and more) recorded from 41 participants under multi-view sensor setups, yielding over 67.72M synchronized frames. The data encompass 62 daily activities spanning structured routines, freestyle behaviors, human-environment interaction, healthcare tasks, etc. All modalities are annotated by high-fidelity 3D pose labels captured via a professional motion-capture system, allowing precise alignment and rich supervision across sensors and views. OctoNet is one of the most comprehensive datasets of its kind, enabling a wide range of learning tasks such as human activity recognition, 3D pose estimation, multi-modal fusion, cross-modal supervision, and sensor foundation models. Extensive experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the sensing capacity using various baselines. OctoNet offers a unique and unified testbed for developing and benchmarking generalizable, robust models for human-centric sensing AI.
